en: In the lower fascicle of the *Wuliangshou jing yiji* (Record of the Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life), it says: "Up to the point where the seven treasures...
[text missing] ...combine to form the substance of the pond. This substance of the pond is also..."
□□□□□□□□□□□□□□ Second, the clarification of the body of the pond:
it is composed of the seven precious jewels.
Third, the clarification of the body of the pond: within this, the characteristics of the phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are explained and elucidated.
The tenth section of the chapter on Emptiness, Impermanence, the Ten Powers, and the Four [Bases of] Self-Assurance,
from the bank of that pond upward.
It covers the surface of the water.
As for these various bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas—
this is the third section within the "Gate of Faithful Exposition."
This explains the Land of Immeasurable Life.
It is exclusively a study of the Mahāyāna, without the distinctions of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Within this chapter, the meaning is further elucidated through six sub-sections.
The first sub-section:
From "If one enters the jeweled pond" down to "desiring to make the water cover the feet until it is pure and formless."
This clarifies that Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas possess great supernormal powers;
they may move at will within the jeweled pond.
If they wish for the water to reach their feet, the water immediately reaches their feet.
This, too, uses a concrete object to express a meaning.
The jewel pond serves as a general metaphor for the teachings and principles of all Buddhas of the three periods of time;
it illustrates how clear water can wash away dust and defilement.
Clear understanding can give rise to insight;
insight can eliminate delusions. Among the various parts of the human body, the feet are considered the lowest;
among the manifold afflictions, the afflictions of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-kleśa*) are the most base.
Now, it is clarified that from the first stage up to the third stage, all afflictions of the vision of truth (dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa) are eliminated,
just as water submerges one's feet; yet,
one desires to have it reach only to the knees.
From the fourth stage through the sixth stage, one exhausts the nine grades of afflictions associated with discursive thought;
this is like water reaching the knees.
To cause it to reach the waist—
The seventh-stage bodhisattva’s severing of craving for the Buddha's merit lies between these two gates,
like water reaching halfway up the waist.
If one wishes for the water to reach the neck, it immediately reaches the neck.
It clarifies that from the eighth stage upward, through to the ninth stage, one enters the quiescence of non-arising, with this realization increasing and becoming clearer in every thought-moment.
One severs the obstacles and afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges until they are exhausted;
only a single grade of subtle ignorance remains, like water submerging the neck with only the head remaining above.
As for the desire to have the body consecrated by sprinkling:
it signifies that on the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), ignorance is completely eliminated,
just as water thoroughly washes the body until it is pure.
"To cause them to return and restore" means that because the transformative manifestations cease and revert to their original state, they are said to "return and restore.
"To harmonize the cold and the warm" means:
It harmonizes the greed, hatred, and delusion of sentient beings—
these three unwholesome roots that cause suffering for sentient beings.
"Opening the spirit and gladdening the body" means:
One should preach the Dharma according to the faculties [of the listeners],
so as to accord with their dispositions. If purity were formless,
then all delusions would be exhausted and there would be no further obstructions or hindrances.
For example, just as space has no distinct forms,
so it is here. The second sub-section, from "The Radiance of Jewels" (*ratnasaṃbhava*) to the end of the chapter titled "Peaceful Bliss" (*sukhāvatī*),

clarifies that when Bodhisattvas or Śrāvakas wish to hear the wondrous sounds of the jewel-pools according to their inclinations— thereby discerning the characteristics of phenomena— the Dharma naturally responds to them accordingly.
As for "the precious sands reflecting with clarity":
this is a metaphor for the final mind of the Great Earth Vajra stage; since its illumination of principle is already all-pervasive, it is equal to that of a Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that there is nothing so profound that it is not illuminated.
"The subtle fragrance returning as a current" refers to entering the cycle of birth and death to engage with sentient beings.
"Transforming and mutually pouring forth" refers to...
This transmits the transformation that causes bodhisattvas of minor practice to advance.
Regarding "neither slow nor fast":
this means that when teaching and engaging with sentient beings, one must proceed from the small to the great and may not speak all at once.
As for "the waves spreading immeasurably":
it refers to manifesting transformations without fixed direction to expound all dharmas;
or, upon hearing the voice of the Buddha, praising the Buddha Jewel.
Those who hear the sound of the Dharma praise the Jewel of the Dharma;
those who hear the sound of the Sangha praise the Jewel of the Sangha.
As for those who hear the sound of "quiescence," it is a praise of nirvana as being quiescent because it is free from entanglements.
As for the sound of "non-self," it means that within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), there is no "I" or "mine."
"Sound of great compassion" means that loving-kindness desires to bestow happiness, while compassion seeks to extract one from suffering.
"Sound of non-action" means...
Within the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no arising or activity of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
This is the third sub-section,
beginning from "Ānanda, those who are reborn in that Buddha-land" and concluding with "the path to *nirvāṇa*."
This clarifies that the worthy and holy ones of that land have attained natural karmic rewards such that,
whenever they desire anything, vessels of the seven precious jewels appear before them in abundance.
Although these foods exist, there are in fact no eaters.
The noble and holy ones clearly manifest and partake of food of a hundred flavors that appears before them;
though they do not consume the taste, they are naturally satiated by merely seeing its color and smelling its fragrance,
their bodies and minds becoming serene and joyful.
This refers to the noble food (ārya-bhojana).
Because it does not possess the flavor of worldly juices, it is said that one "does not eat.
This is the fourth sub-section.
From those śrāvakas and bodhisattvas up to the ultimate, infinite essence—
this clarifies that in the pure Mahāyāna practice there is no differentiation between the three vehicles.
Those who are moved [by this teaching] belong to the same category.
This clarifies the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, humans,
and devas; these three types of great beings possess lofty and brilliant wisdom.
Practicing the Mahāyāna together, all myriad virtues converge;
because there is no other destination, they are called "of the same class. As for "their forms having no different appearances": [this means that their physical manifestations are uniform].
His body is the color of purple-polished gold and possesses the thirty-two marks;
these marks and secondary characteristics are perfectly symmetrical, and his proportions are likewise even.
Because he accords with other directions, he bears the names "Heavenly" and "Human."
Those who practice the Mahāyāna together have no threefold distinction.
Because they accord with the Sahā world, there are the names "deva" and "human.
Although the names are three, their practice is identical within the One Vehicle.
Regarding "neither deva nor human":
their physical forms and faculties are upright, refined, subtle, and extraordinary;
they do not belong to the categories of either devas or humans.
"All receive a body of spontaneous emptiness" clarifies that this body is empty and subtle,
externally radiant and transparent like light or a shadow.
"The ultimate essence" refers to—
His body is immeasurably large and his lifespan is likewise long.
This is the fifth sub-section,
beginning from "For example, like a poor beggar in the world" and ending with "a hundred thousand million billion times incalculable."
The countenance of the Great Being of the Western Quarter is so upright and handsome that it is peerless in the world.

Even if one were to compare the rulers of this land up to the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), against him, they would not equal even a hundred thousand million billionth part of his splendor.
It does not equal even one part [of the merit].
Thus, we know that it is because of the long duration of kalpas since the past that one now attains this wondrous and supreme retribution.
The sixth subsection:
From the description of the clothing, food, and drink of the devas and humans in the Land of Immeasurable Life until the end of the fascicle,
this clarifies the karmic fruits experienced by the humans and devas of that land.
The seven natural treasures are enjoyed according to one’s wishes;
these are no different from the fruits of retribution obtained by the various bodhisattvas.
This concludes the summary of the fruits of retribution for the Pure Land gate, answering the vows among the aforementioned forty-eight vows that encompass those of humans and devas.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for those sentient beings who are born in that land"—this is the third section of the correct exposition, which praises and encourages cultivation.
The preceding chapter clarified the causes and conditions for that Buddha’s long life.
Those of sharp faculties immediately receive understanding and awakening, yet those of dull faculties are still unable to comprehend it.
For this reason, the Buddhas of the ten directions mutually respond to one another,
praising that Buddha’s long life span and the utter purity of his land in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
Exhorting and inducing through the sublime joys of devas and humans:
those of dull faculties diligently cultivate sublime causes to obtain sublime fruits.
Within this section on the gate of exhortation to practice, there are generally ten points explaining the meaning of the exhortations to practice.
First is the exhortation to practice:
first praising that Buddha,
and then expressing the aspiration of the three grades of sentient beings in this land to be born in that country.
The second section is the exhortation to practice,
clarifying how bodhisattvas from the ten directions travel to the western land to receive and praise the sublime Dharma, and cause it to circulate throughout the ten directions.
The third is the exhortation to practice,
clarifying that Avalokiteśvara will succeed him as the next Buddha in this very life,
no different from [the case of] Amitāyus.
The fourth is the exhortation to practice,
clarifying how Amitāyus Buddha delivers sentient beings by preaching the Dharma for them.
The fifth [section] on exhortation to practice extensively clarifies the gains and losses of sentient beings.
The sixth [section] on exhortation to practice provides a clear and concise explanation.
The seventh exhortation to practice clarifies the violation of the pure precepts.
The eighth exhortation to practice...
The "Clarifying Sincerity" is an exhortation.
The ninth is the exhortation to practice.
The "Clarifying the Vast Manifestation of Buddha-lands" is [the tenth].
The tenth is the exhortation to practice,
which clarifies the understanding of the precepts.
The first is the exhortation to practice.
As for those sentient beings who are born in that land from this world,
the causes for their birth have long been established; having already developed the aspiration for enlightenment,
they have attained faith as the foremost of the five faculties and these are firmly established.
Within the state of non-retrogression, there is the provisional designation of the accomplishment of emptiness.

These are persons of the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). This corresponds to the forty-eighth vow among the preceding vows: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not all abide within the stage of right determination."
Why is this so? As for the reason why those who abide in the group of the rightly determined (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi) do so,
it is because they have fallen into the group of the rightly determined precisely due to the correctness of the causes they have cultivated.
Regarding "there being no groups of the heterodox":
that land is pure and free from all false views,
such as committing the five heinous crimes or slandering the Vaipulya sutras.
As for those in the indeterminate group,
they do not fall back from right practice to engage in wrong conduct.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [protect them].
Regarding the phrase "all together praise and extol Amitāyus Buddha":
this clarifies why it is necessary to praise Amitāyus Buddha.
It is for the sake of the dispositions of the time, so as to cause the arising of a longing and yearning, whereby one applies oneself to the causal practices and attains the fruit.
Regarding "majestic spiritual power and merit":
"majesty" refers to external virtues,
while "spiritual power" refers to internal virtues.
The Sage’s wisdom is manifested externally as majestic power that comes to benefit others; internally, its resolution is what constitutes the "spiritual" (*shen*).
As for "merit" (*gongde*):
because one attains this goodness through the cultivation of effort and progressive practice, it is called merit.
Any sentient beings who hear his name and feel faith and joy for even a single moment— beings who,
upon hearing praises of that land’s pure and wondrous bliss,
all give rise to a sincere mind and maintain it in continuous succession, vowing to be born in that land.
Regarding those who, with a sincere mind, dedicate their merit and vow to be born in that land:
if one speaks of the nature of goodness and the arising of its causes and conditions in isolation,
there would naturally be the attainment of the fruit, yet there would be no need for dedication.
If one is bound by the karmic retribution of further aggregates (skandhas) and material wealth,
there is no possibility of turning back [from saṃsāra].
That which allows for the possibility of turning back is as follows:
I dedicate the karmic fruit of my attainment to all sentient beings.
Through the merit of this dedication, I give rise to goodness;
as that goodness increases, [it leads to further realization].
The karmic retribution bound to them is then severed;
once the coarse retribution is severed,
one attains a subtle and wondrous body.
It is called "dedication" because it turns back what is coarse to produce what is subtle.
Regarding "abiding in non-retrogression," the mind of dedication serves as the cause.
In the end, one attains non-retrogression as the fruit.

Regarding the vow to be born in that land, there are three grades of practitioners; the following clarifies how the devas and people of the ten directions who have resolved their minds and focused their devotion vow to be born in that land.
Those who wish to be born there are generally of three classes.
These three classes of persons are distinguished by three grades: superior, middling, and inferior.
Although this scriptural passage briefly distinguishes these three grades, its meaning implicitly contains nine.
Now, following the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, the three grades are extensively explained and divided into nine ranks;
the Buddha himself has interpreted them clearly and distinctly.
As for those of the superior grade:
Generally, there are nine grades of persons born into this world.
Those of the highest grade attain rebirth as soon as they give rise to three kinds of mind.
What are the three?
First, the sincere mind;
second, the profound mind.
Third is the mind of dedication and aspiration.
One who possesses these three minds will certainly be born in that land.
Having left home, abandoned desire, and become a śramaṇa, [one should cultivate them].
Those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta are individuals of the highest caliber;
they vow to be born in that land.
He immediately renounced worldly desires to leave the household life, gave rise to the bodhicitta, and practiced loving-kindness and non-killing.
He observed all the precepts, recited the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras,
cultivated the six remembrances, and made vows to be reborn [in the Pure Land].
Possessing these merits, from the first day up to the seventh,
they practice with diligent vigor, without ceasing day or night. Amitābha Buddha,
together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, and the great assembly of devas, [will appear].
All were riding in palaces made of the seven treasures;
Avalokiteśvara held a vajra platform together with Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Upon reaching the person's presence,
Amitābha Buddha emits a great radiance that illumines their body,
and together with the various bodhisattvas, he extends his hand to welcome them.
They praise the practitioner and exhort their mind toward progress.
Upon seeing this, the practitioner rejoices and leaps for joy,
perceiving themselves as riding upon a vajra pedestal.
Following behind the Buddha,
they will be reborn in that land in the time it takes to snap one's fingers,
where they shall behold the body of that Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattvas, all endowed with perfect marks.
He preached the sublime Dharma within the Forest of Radiance;
having heard it, he immediately realized the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
He traveled throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas.
Having received successive predictions of enlightenment in the presence of all the Buddhas,
he returned to his own land and attained immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharani-doors.
This is called a person of the highest grade.
As for those who single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitābha Buddha,
these are persons of the middle grade among the superior class who aspire to be born in that land.
This person need not necessarily uphold, receive, read, or recite the Vaipulya sutras;
yet they skillfully understand their meaning and intent,
and their mind is not startled or shaken by the ultimate truth.
With deep faith in cause and effect, do not slander the Mahāyāna.
By virtue of these merits, may you be reborn in that land.
At the time of death, when your life comes to an end—
Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and an immeasurable multitude,
all holding purple-golden platforms, appeared before that person and praised them, saying:
Dharma-heir:
"Just as one who practices the Mahāyāna understands the primary meaning (paramārtha),
so do I now welcome and uphold you."
Simultaneously, a thousand transformation Buddhas extend their hands to him;
the practitioner sees himself seated within a purple-gold pedestal,
joining his palms in homage and praising all the Buddhas.
In the space of a single thought-moment, one is immediately born within a pond of the seven treasures in that land;
after one night has passed, the precious lotus flower finally opens,
and the practitioner’s body becomes the color of purple-polished gold.
Beneath their feet were lotus flowers made of the seven precious gems.
The Buddha and the bodhisattvas simultaneously emitted light,
which illuminated the bodies of those people, causing the eyes of those walking there to open and become clear.
Due to their past habitual tendencies, they were able to hear various sounds,
all of which were the profound and supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The practitioner then descended from the golden terrace, prostrated before the Buddha, joined his palms, and praised the World-Honored One.
After seven days had passed,
he attained the stage of non-retrogression and was immediately able to fly to the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas.
By practicing various samādhis under the presence of the Buddhas,
one attains the realization of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and receives a prediction of enlightenment within one minor kalpa.
This is called the person of middle capacity among those of the highest grade.
Regarding those who cultivate various merits and vow to be born in that land:
these are the people of the lower grade among the superior class who vow to be born in that land.
Such persons also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna.
One should simply give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and dedicate this merit with the vow to be reborn in that land.
When the practitioner is on the verge of death,
Amitābha Buddha, together with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
holding golden lotus flowers along with various bodhisattvas,
manifested as five hundred Buddhas.
To welcome this practitioner,
five hundred transformation Buddhas simultaneously extended their hands and praised him, saying:
"O Son of the Dharma!"
"Now that you have purely resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment,
I come to welcome you. Thereupon,
the practitioner sees himself seated upon a lotus flower.
Once they have sat down, the flowers close;
they then follow behind the Buddha and are reborn in that land within a pond of the seven treasures.
After one day and one night has passed, the lotus flower opens.
Within seven days, he was finally able to see the Buddha;
yet, although he beheld the Buddha’s body, his mind was not yet clearly enlightened regarding its manifold marks and signs.
Only after twenty-one days did he see them with perfect clarity.
Having heard [the Dharma] pervading the ten directions, he made offerings to all Buddhas.
Before those Buddhas, he heard the profoundly deep teachings of the mind.
After three minor kalpas, he attained the Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas.
They dwell on the Stage of Joy;
these are called those of the lower grade among the superior class.
These sentient beings, at the time their lives come to an end, [attain rebirth] as described in the general summary of the three grades of persons in the text of the superior class.
They follow the Buddha and dwell there, being born through spontaneous transformation.
Among those of the middle grade,
there are likewise people of superior, middling, and inferior capacities.
Although they are unable to practice as śramaṇas, they extensively cultivate meritorious deeds;
these are those of the highest grade among laypeople in the middle class who aspire to be born in that land.
They uphold the five precepts, the eight precepts, and the fast-day observances.
By not committing the five heinous crimes and remaining free from all faults and afflictions,
one dedicates these roots of goodness with the vow to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
At the moment of death, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus, will appear.
He emitted golden light that reached before the person and expounded upon suffering,
emptiness, impermanence, and non-self,
praising the renunciation of home life as the means to be freed from all sufferings.
Upon seeing this, the person’s heart was filled with great joy;
beholding himself seated upon a lotus pedestal,
he knelt upright with palms joined and paid homage to the Buddha.
In the mere moment of raising one's head, one attains rebirth in that land.
The lotus flower then opens,
and one hears various voices praising the Four Noble Truths.
He immediately attains the path of Arhatship,
endowed with the three insights, the six supernatural powers, and the eight liberations;
this is called the person of the upper grade among those of the middle class.
"One who single-mindedly and exclusively recollects Amitāyus Buddha" refers to a person of middle capacity within the Middle Grade who aspires to be born in that land;
this clarifies the practitioner.
If one observes the eightfold precepts for one day and one night,
or observes the śrāmaṇera precepts and the full ordination (upasampadā) for one day and one night.
With his deportment flawless,
he dedicates these merits toward the aspiration to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
perfuming his cultivation with the fragrance of the precepts.
When this practitioner is on the verge of death,
they will see Amitābha Buddha together with his retinue emitting golden light and holding a lotus flower made of the seven precious gems, approaching the person. The practitioner...
He saw a voice in the sky praising him, saying:
"O son of good family!
You are a virtuous person such as this."
"In accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time,
I have come to welcome you.
The practitioner then sees his own body seated upon a lotus flower.
The lotus flower immediately closed and was born in the west within a precious pond;
after seven days had passed,
the lotus flower then blossomed.
Once the flowers had fully blossomed,
he opened his eyes, joined his palms, and praised the World-Honored One;
hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
After half a kalpa, they have already attained the path of Arhatship;
these are the people of the middle grade within the middle class.
Those who practice good deeds to a moderate degree and, having observed the fasts and precepts, scatter flowers and burn incense [are included here].
This refers to those of the lowest grade in the middle class who vow to be born in that land.
It clarifies that these practitioners filially support their parents and practice worldly benevolence and goodness.
When this person was on the verge of death,
they encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
who extensively expounded for them the wondrous bliss of the land of Amitābha Buddha.
He also preached for him the forty-eight vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
Having heard this matter, he immediately passed away,
as quickly as a person bends and extends their arm.
They will immediately be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss,
where after seven days they will encounter Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
hearing the Dharma, they will rejoice.
After the passing of one small kalpa, they will attain the path of Arhatship;
these are called those of the lower grade in the middle class.
By dedicating this merit with the vow to be born in that land, they will eventually be as described above for those of the superior class.
This generally clarifies that those of the three grades among the middle class who vow to be born in the Western Land will be met by that Buddha and his great assembly to welcome them.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Among those of the lower class, there are likewise people of superior, middling, and inferior grades."
If one is unable to perform various meritorious deeds,
yet should resolve to attain unexcelled bodhicitta,
this clarifies that such a person of inferior capacity aspires to be born in that land.
Or, though they do not slander the Vaipulya sutras, they commit various evil deeds;
such foolish people create many unwholesome dharmas without any sense of shame or remorse.
When their life was about to end, they encountered virtuous friends who praised the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Because they were able to hear the names of these various sūtras, [they attained rebirth].
This eliminates the grave sins of a thousand kalpas.
Furthermore, the wise one instructs them to join their palms and hands,
and recite the name of Namu Amida Butsu.
Fifty billion kalpas of the offenses of birth and death were thereby eliminated.
At that time, that Buddha dispatched emanated Buddhas, emanated Avalokiteśvara, and emanated Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Approaching the practitioner, he praised him, saying:
"O son of good family,
because you have invoked the name of the Buddha, all your transgressions are extinguished."
"I have come to welcome you.
Having spoken these words,
the practitioner immediately saw the light of the transformed Buddha pervading his entire room.
Having seen this, they rejoice and immediately pass away;
riding upon jeweled lotuses,
they follow behind the emanation buddhas and are reborn within a pool of the seven treasures.
After seven weeks have passed, the lotus flower finally blooms.
At the moment the flower blooms,
Avalokiteśvara emits a great radiance and stands before that person.
For their sake, he preached the profound twelvefold canon of sutras; having heard them, they believed and understood, giving rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed path.
After ten minor kalpas, they perfected the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas and attained entry into the first stage.
These are persons of the superior grade among the lowest class.
Those who single-mindedly and exclusively focus their intent, even for as little as ten recitations, upon Amitāyus Buddha,
are persons of the middle grade among the lowest class.
This practitioner may violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of monastic precepts;
such a person is a fool.
They steal the property of the Saṃgha;
they pilfer the goods belonging to the present Saṃgha;
they preach the Dharma impurely, devoid of shame and remorse.
Adorned with various transgressions,
such a sinner, due to the arousal of evil, ought to fall into hell.
When his life was about to end,
the various fires of hell arrived all at once;
he then encountered a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
For their sake, he spoke of the ten powers and majestic virtue of Amitābha Buddha;
he extensively explained that Buddha’s radiance and spiritual power, and also praised his morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Upon hearing this, that person shall be freed from the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
The fierce fires of hell will transform into cool breezes,
blowing celestial flowers upon them.
Upon each flower are transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who welcome this person,
as if in the space of a single thought-moment.
He immediately attains rebirth within a pond of the seven treasures;
there, amidst a lotus flower, he remains for six kalpas before the flower finally opens.
Avalokiteśvara, of great power and resolve,
shall comfort those people with a Brahma-like voice and preach for them the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
Having heard this Dharma, they immediately resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path;
these are the people of middle capacity among the lower grade.
If, upon hearing the profound Dharma, they rejoice with faith and delight, giving rise to no doubt or confusion—
This refers to those of the lowest grade within the lowest class who aspire to be born in that land.
It clarifies that these practitioners have previously committed unwholesome deeds, such as the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts.
Possessing all manner of unwholesome deeds,
they will inevitably fall into the evil realms,
where they shall undergo endless suffering throughout many kalpas.
When such an evil person approaches the end of life and encounters a spiritual friend who provides various forms of consolation,
that friend preaches the sublime Dharma and instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
When a practitioner sees themselves oppressed by suffering and has no leisure to recollect the Buddha,
a spiritual friend says to that person:
"If you cannot recite silently..."
Simply raise your voice and call upon the Buddha of Immeasurable Life.
In this way, with a sincere mind, let the sound not cease until you have completed ten recitations.
In every moment of thought, one eliminates the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
After the end of life, one shall see a golden lotus flower, like a wheel of the sun, appearing before that person.
In a single moment of thought, one immediately attains rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss;
there, within a lotus flower, twelve great kalpas must pass before the flower finally opens.
Avalokiteśvara Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with a voice of great compassion,
shall extensively expound for that person the Dharma of the true mark and the method for extinguishing sinful karma.
Upon hearing this, the practitioner gives rise to joy and immediately resolves upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi.
This is called the person of the lowest grade within the lower class.
"Without giving rise to doubt,
even for a single thought-moment" means that one's mind,
even in a single thought-moment, remains settled and clear, such that no uncertainty arises.
If there is any doubt that the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows of Amitāyus Buddha swirls like five Mount Sumerus,
one might give rise to a doubting thought,
wondering: "Is this white tuft of hair actually like five Mount Sumerus?"
"Or perhaps it does not exist?
As soon as such a thought arises, one falls into the city of doubt.
For twelve kalpas, one must diligently repent and practice the Path.
After twelve full kalpas, one shall emerge from the city of doubt and first ascend to the stage of non-retrogression.
As for this person who dreams of that Buddha at the time of death:
From this point downward, the text generally clarifies that people of the three grades of capacity aspire to be born in that land.
The second section, "Exhortation to Practice," extends from the passage beginning with "The majestic spiritual power of Amitāyus Buddha is infinite" until the verses of praise.
Bodhisattvas from the ten directions go to the western quarter to hear and receive the sublime Dharma and to propagate the true teaching.
There are no Buddhas, Tathāgatas, who do not praise it.
The reason all Buddhas jointly praise that Buddha is precisely to lead ordinary beings and bodhisattvas by following his example;
thus they travel to that land to listen to and receive the Dharma,
proclaiming what has not yet been heard.
Regarding the statement, "At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse," there are thirty verses in total below this;
all of them are Śākyamuni’s verses extolling the virtues of that Buddha.
In general, this verse is explained through four stages.
The first consists of seven lines,
which collectively praise the bodhisattvas of the ten directions for making offerings of flowers, incense, and music, and for their aspiration to attain a pure land.
It is no different from the West.
The second section, beginning with "From the Immeasurable Honored One who Responds to the Occasion," consists of eight lines below this;
it clarifies that the Buddha responds to their request.
This explains that by practicing sublime conduct, one will certainly attain the pure fruit.
The third section, from "The Buddhas address the Bodhisattvas" onwards, consists of eight lines and clarifies how the Buddhas of the ten directions praise the various Bodhisattvas.
This causes one to cultivate the myriad practices in order to approach that land.
Fourth, from "Whether Śrāvakas or Bodhisattvas" below this point until the end of the verse,
it clarifies that the Buddha’s wisdom is profound and far-reaching, beyond the measurement of the two vehicles or the ten stages.
Regarding the first stage, as for the various Buddha-lands in the eastern direction:
the following two verses clarify that Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges dwell in those lands.
Each brings celestial, wondrous flowers.
The following two verses clarify how the Bodhisattvas bring exquisite flowers and music as offerings to the Buddha.
"Thoroughly attaining the wisdom of supernormal powers"—
the following two verses praise the Buddha’s wisdom as being profound and far-reaching, beyond compare.
"Beholding that adorned pure land"—
this single verse clarifies that the Bodhisattva beholds the pure land of the West;
the aspiration to attain such a pure land through the arousal of the bodhicitta is likewise.
In the second stage, at the appropriate time, the World-Honored One Amitāyus—
through these following two verses— manifests a guest smile and emits light as a preliminary to bestowing the pure fruit upon those who aspire to it.
"The Great Being Avalokiteśvara"—
this single verse clarifies that Avalokiteśvara responds to sentient beings' capacities by granting their requests.
His Brahma-voice resounds like a peal of thunder.
This verse clarifies that as Amitābha Buddha is about to preach the Dharma,
he first issues a solemn admonition to ensure a profound and reverent state of mind:
"O noble sons who have come from the ten directions."
The following four verses explain that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams;
if one can deeply penetrate this principle, the Pure Land may then be attained.
In the third stage, the Buddhas address the Bodhisattvas;
these two verses exhort people to resolve to be born in that land,
clarifying that the Buddhas of the ten directions cause all Bodhisattvas to receive their predictions and attain pure, wondrous lands.
"By the power of that Buddha’s original vow"—
this single verse clarifies that for those who are reborn through the power of the original vows of Amitāyus Buddha, there is benefit.
"The Bodhisattva gives rise to the supreme vow."
The following two verses exhort one to cultivate pure causes,
which will inevitably result in pure fruits;
the retribution obtained will not differ from that of the Western Land.
If a person lacks the roots of goodness,
these following three verses clarify that those who are able to cultivate the causes can hear that sublime Dharma,
whereas those who do not cultivate the causes cannot hear this Dharma.
The fourth stage exhorts śrāvakas or bodhisattvas not to attempt to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom by means of their own deliberation;
it clarifies that since śrāvakas and bodhisattvas cannot measure the Buddha’s wisdom,
how much less can ordinary beings do so.
Having compared the wisdom of the śrāvakas— who are like blind men—
to the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, which is deep, vast, boundless, and bottomless,
these four verses praise the Buddha’s wisdom as being difficult to fathom.
Longevity is also difficult to obtain;
it is not only longevity that is difficult to obtain,
for it is also difficult to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Not only is it difficult to encounter a Buddha appearing in the world,
but it is also difficult to give rise to faith upon encountering a Buddha.
However, if one possesses wisdom, it is easy to give rise to faith.
Without wisdom, it is difficult.
Third is the exhortation to practice.
This begins from the Buddha’s address to Ānanda regarding the bodhisattvas of that land and concludes with the manifestation that they are identical to those in our own land.
It clarifies that the stages of Avalokiteśvara and others correspond to the ten bhūmis;
in a single lifetime, they will succeed the Buddha and are well able to come and go to guide and receive sentient beings.
"Except for those who have made a fundamental vow for the sake of sentient beings" clarifies that in the past,
Avalokiteśvara established karmic connections with the beings of this Sahā world,
and thus his life-force returns to respond to their rebirth.
However, this bodhisattva is fundamentally formless, yet manifests forms in response to sentient beings;
now that the forms manifested in response to sentient beings have been eliminated, it is said that "only those resulting from original vows are excluded.
Thus, they adorn themselves with the merit of their great vows.
The physical body functions to transform sentient beings,
causing them to be liberated from the manifold sufferings of the three realms. What are these four?
First, to cause those who have not yet understood to understand;
second, to cause those who have not yet crossed over to cross over;
third, to cause those who have not yet found peace to find peace.
Fourth, it causes those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa to attain it.
Among them, there are two bodhisattvas who are most honored and foremost:
one is Avalokiteśvara.
The second is Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
These two bodhisattvas possess lofty and far-reaching virtuous conduct and are next in line to succeed the Buddha;
therefore, they are called "foremost."
Regarding these two bodhisattvas who, at the end of their lives, undergo transformation and are reborn in that land:
this clarifies that Avalokiteśvara will cast off this body, be reborn in the Western Land, and attain Buddhahood;
it is for this reason that Śākyamuni offers praise.
These two bodhisattvas, upon casting off their lives, manifested the attainment of Buddhahood;
the lands they obtained were pure, sublime, and blissful.
This clarifies that these Great Beings are fundamentally formless from the outset.
What is it that they relinquish?
It is merely manifested in order to conform to the sentiments of the common people;
for when their lives end, the multitude sees these two Great Beings relinquishing their lives and being reborn in that Buddha-field.

"Deepening one's resolve and wishing in its entirety to be reborn in that land" means that those whose wisdom is perfected and who have penetrated all phenomena to their ultimate essence and subtlety clarify that sentient beings travel to that land and practice the Way for a long duration.
One enters the wisdom of the equality of non-arising;
upon its fulfillment, one ascends to the first bhūmi.
Regarding "unimpeded supernormal powers," this refers to one who possesses the six abhijñās.
"Freedom of flight" means mastery over movement.
"The faculties are clear and sharp" means that spiritual wisdom penetrates all things, transcending all boundaries to benefit others.
As for those of dull faculties who accomplish the two types of patience, they accomplish the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) and the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*).
This indicates that such persons abide in the lower thirty minds, having long planted the causes and diligently cultivated the ten thousand practices.
Having fulfilled their vows for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to be born in that land,
they pass through the two patiences (*kṣānti*) and ascend to the sixth stage (*bhūmi*).
Those of sharp faculties, however, abide in the fulfillment of the lower thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*).
Having also diligently cultivated the myriad practices for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
his faculties became further sharpened; wishing to be born in that land,
he immediately ascended to the stage of the eighth bhūmi and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
They have also passed through the stages of the lower grounds.
From that land, the bodhisattvas, having received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, returned to their own lands.
This clarifies the swiftness of the supernormal powers attained by bodhisattvas as they desire to travel to the ten directions.
Regarding the fourth exhortation to practice: when making offerings to the Buddhas, one need not carry incense or flowers to those Buddha-lands;
by simply recollecting them, one obtains offerings according to one's wishes.
From the passage "The Buddha of Immeasurable Life, for the sake of the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas...
onwards, it clarifies that Amitābha Buddha extensively expounds the wondrous Dharma beneath trees made of the seven precious jewels.
He sighed as the seven treasures produced the sounds of the five musical notes.
Within these sounds, he articulated the tones of gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu, as well as the sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Upon hearing these sounds, all attained awakening to the Way.
From the passage beginning "The various bodhisattvas who have been born in that buddha-land" onwards,
it clarifies that these bodhisattvas are internally endowed with inexhaustible dharmas and are externally able to preach the Dharma for others with sovereign mastery.
Regarding this chapter, there are three sub-sections that clarify its meaning.
As for "conforming to wisdom," this clarifies the three types of action (karma) of a bodhisattva.
He practices bodily action in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom;
he practices verbal action in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom;
he practices mental action in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom.
It is to practice in accordance with the Buddha’s wisdom.
"Without transgression and without failure" clarifies that there is no failure in body, no failure in speech, and no failure in mind.
Regarding the fact that all things within that land are devoid of the notion of "mine," this section below praises the three roots of goodness and consists of four phrases.
This clarifies that in the eighth stage, one is free from the greed of the mental ground and illuminates the principle of non-arising;
thus, one perceives neither a self that can receive nor a self that can grasp.
Being indistinct and without marks,
how could there be any greed or desire to be found?
One who possesses a mind free from defiled attachment—
If there were afflictions within that perceive an object,
there would be attachment arising;
since there are no afflictions within, what external thing could possibly defile it?
One who has abandoned the mind of coming and going and whose emotions are unattached possesses no poverty within;
externally, they are able to manifest transformations at will.
To act with spontaneous mastery, having no partiality toward either the favored or the unfavored,
means that a response occurs whenever there is an occasion for it, without bias;
it is for this reason that one says there is no partiality toward either the favored or the unfavored.
"Neither that nor self" refers to these four phrases which clarify the absence of ill-will.
"Neither competing nor litigating" refers to...
Regarding the second phrase:
if one were on the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there might be disputes and litigation;
however, this clarifies that the minds of Bodhisattvas on these eight stages have realized the principle of the equality of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
How could there be any anger in one who possesses virtue?
For those who have attained a mind of great compassion and the intent to benefit all sentient beings—
this is the third phrase.
This clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s internal virtue consists of compassion for the salvation of suffering sentient beings;
they constantly practice a mind of benefit,
clearly understanding how to remain free from anger, being gentle, disciplined, and devoid of resentment.
The fourth phrase:
if stubborn and unruly sentient beings are subdued with gentle and harmonious speech,
one teaches them and causes them to enter the right path.
Nor does it give rise to anger.
To be free from hindrances, pure, and without weariness or indolence—
this below clarifies the absence of encountering delusion.
Having departed from the delusions and obscurations of the three realms, one attains a pure mind.
Because one clarifies the mind and exerts oneself with diligent application, there is no mind of weariness or indolence.
As for the "equal mind":
It is the mind of equanimity.
The "superior mind" refers to the mind of non-arising at the eighth stage.
It is called "superior" because it seeks the higher stages.
As for the "profound mind," it enters the principle of non-arising and quiescent extinction.
Progressing in every thought-moment is the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
As for the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*):
To remain within the object without distraction.
One whose mind loves the Dharma, delights in the Dharma,
and rejoices in the Dharma begins by giving rise to the thought that contemplates the object as being seen through craving.
The object should be taken as joy by the mind;
because it is a single, undifferentiated appearance in which no distinction is seen, it is the mind that delights in the Dharma.
This is the mind that extinguishes all afflictions and departs from the evil realms.
To extinguish the three realms or their defilements means to bring to ultimate completion all that is practiced by Bodhisattvas;
it means to bring to ultimate completion the practice of the ten stages (bhūmi).
Those who attain profound meditative concentration do not merely understand the four dhyānas;
they penetrate deeply into the four formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).
These are the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding those who possess the various penetrations, clarities, and wisdoms:
"penetrations" refers to the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*).
This is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Clarity" refers to the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), by which wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to make decisive judgments.
"Wandering with the will toward the seven factors of awakening" means:
In the Śrāvaka vehicle, one practices the seven factors of enlightenment;
from the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin up to Arhat, the afflictions of conceptualization are completely severed.
In the Bodhisattva vehicle, one practices the seven factors of enlightenment from the fourth bhūmi through the seventh bhūmi.
Furthermore, because they have severed discursive thought and exhausted the afflictions, they are categorized as the seven factors of enlightenment.
What are these seven? First is the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
The discernment of all phenomena is the grasping of the most excellent dharma.
Second is the awakening of diligence,
which consists of ceaselessly and diligently examining [the mind] day and night within the context of contemplation.
Third is the awakening factor of joy:
attaining right contemplation, one experiences immeasurable gladness within the mind.
Fourth is the awakening factor of mindfulness.
It is the increasing clarity in every moment of thought.
Fifth is the awakening of concentration (*samādhi*).
Concentration is the fruit of mindfulness; it is the mind abiding upon its object without distraction.

Sixth is the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*); this clarifies that the experience of bliss is solely due to serenity. Seventh is the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
"Abandoning the coarse and subtle delusions of the three realms" means their exhaustion.
Regarding "the fleshly eye being clear and penetrating," there are five kinds of eyes within this context.
The first four eyes are established based on the causal stage (*hetubhūmi*),
while the latter single eye has its locus in the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*).
If one does not distinguish them as object and wisdom, they would be merely a single *prajñā-cakṣus*.
If it were not so, there would be only one eye— the object of the Dharma-eye;
that which is illuminated is wisdom,
and that which illuminates constitutes the four eyes based on their respective natures.
Within the Eye of Dharma, setting aside the three eyes that perceive forms, that which is called the "eye" refers to the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*).
Regarding the objects of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), there are both coarse and subtle;
the fleshly eye perceives the coarse.
The divine eye perceives the sublime.
Among the fourteen kinds of form, only one kind of form is coarse and is therefore seen by the fleshly eye;
the remaining thirteen kinds of form are subtle and sublime, and thus belong to what is perceived by the divine eye.
Among the phenomena of causes and conditions, there is nothing that surpasses existence and non-existence.
"Existence" refers to form, which belongs to what is seen by the physical eye;
"non-existence" refers to the Dharma-body and Buddha-nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This is the wondrous existence.
To illuminate both wondrous existence and wondrous non-existence is called the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*).

To illuminate the four aggregates (*skandha*)—which are neither form nor mind, nor mental factors (*caitta*), as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) and outflowing or non-outflowing formations—is different from the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).
The coarseness of the divine eye does not equal the subtlety of the wisdom eye.
Not subsumed by these three eyes,
it returns to being designated by the name "dharma-eye."
The fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) receive their names according to their faculties;
the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) is designated based on its object;
and the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) is named after the essence of wisdom itself.
The four eyes do not encompass all that is seen; their vision of forms is incomplete.
Even when they illuminate emptiness, they have not yet exhausted its source or fully realized its nature.
Only the Buddha is thus capable.
This is because it is the Buddha-eye of Kāśyapa.

Regarding the statement that "the fleshly eye is so clear and penetrating that there is nothing it does not discern," this clarifies that the fleshly eye perceives only coarse forms and does not reach the subtle forms.
Regarding the supernormal power of the divine eye that penetrates the immeasurable and limitless:
this is because the clear divine eye perceives subtle forms with lucidity;
thus, "penetration" refers to penetration in specific instances, not universal penetration across all places.
These two eyes receive their names from their respective faculties and are established within thirty mental states.
As for the Dharma-eye that observes the ultimate paths,
this Dharma-eye is clarified from the first stage through the seventh stage.
This Dharma-eye encompasses all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, including both those that are subject to causal conditions and those not subject to causal conditions,
such as the unmanifest Buddha-nature and other such dharmas.
The wisdom-eye perceives the truth and is able to cross over to the further shore.
This wisdom-eye extends from the eighth stage to the tenth stage.
Wisdom is able to discern emptiness and realize the principle of true suchness (*tathatā*) as non-arising;
because it is proximate to the fruit of Buddhahood, it is able to cross over that shore.
One who fully awakens to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) through the perfection of the Buddha-eye—
this single eye is the Buddha-eye;
it is the perfection of the five eyes.
He has awakened to all phenomena of existence and non-existence such that nothing is not clearly manifest.
From the descent of the Great Illumination into the Vajra [nature] until now, none have attained this eye;
only upon attaining Buddhahood shall one truly realize it. It is he who, with unimpeded wisdom, expounds it for the sake of others.
The Tathāgata, by means of the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence— eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), phrasing (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*),
and ready speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)— constantly expounds the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
He contemplates the three realms as empty and devoid of anything that exists.
All phenomena within the three realms are entirely false;
not a single phenomenon is real. Those who aspire to seek the Buddha-dharma and possess all forms of eloquence do not perceive even a single phenomenon within the three realms as worthy of delight.
He then sought the Tathāgata’s true and wondrous scriptures so as to be endowed with the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
To eliminate the afflictions and sufferings of sentient beings,
the Tathāgata possesses the power of immeasurable wisdom.
It removes the afflictions and sufferings of sentient beings.
Those born from the Tathāgata are so called because their wisdom and eloquence from the eighth stage upward are obtained from the Tathāgata.
It is said that they are born from the Tathāgata.
Regarding those who understand the suchness of dharmas,
this clarifies that from the eighth stage upward, their understanding is identical to that of the Buddha.
They are skillfully able to manifest and appear in the form of a Buddha to preach the Dharma;
because they act in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, it is said that they understand the suchness (tathatā) of phenomena.
They are those who have well cultivated the skillful means of the sounds of cessation through wisdom.
They skillfully know how to manifest sounds beyond the three realms to receive and guide sentient beings through the cessation of habitual tendencies.
Those who cultivate the roots of all goodness and whose resolve honors the Buddha-way cultivate mindfulness and diligence to revere the fruit of Buddhahood.
To know that all phenomena are entirely quiescent means that they have never had the nature of arising;
because one does not perceive the marks of existence or non-existence,
they are called "quiescent."
Regarding "the afflictions of the birth-body and the two remaining types are both exhausted":
that which is born within the three realms is the cause;
the body itself is the fruit.
Afflictions and karma serve as the cause,
while the body of the five aggregates within birth and death serves as the effect.
This clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage eliminate the body of segmented retribution within the triple world.
The first is the removal of the coarse afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms; this is the second.
These two types of coarse retribution (*vipāka*) remain as remnants until the edge of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Now, because these two remaining coarse retributions are eliminated at the eighth stage, it is said that "the two remnants are both exhausted."
Furthermore, another interpretation holds that regarding the two types of afflictions of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*),
while the others are all exhausted, these remaining subtle habitual afflictions exist outside the three realms;
only Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage are able to sever them completely.
It should be understood that these subtle habitual tendencies have two remaining types:
first, the remainder of karma;
second, the remainder of afflictions.

The reason for saying "the remainder" is that while Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage have indeed exhausted the coarse [defilements] of the three realms— the coarse internal karma and coarse afflictions—
they have not yet severed the subtle habitual tendencies of the *avidyā-āvasthā* (ground of ignorance) outside the three realms; therefore, it is called "the remainder."

The statement that "the afflictions of the birth-body and the two remaining [categories] are all exhausted" clarifies that while the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage has already severed their own portion [of afflictions],
they have not yet been able to sever the portions belonging to the ninth and tenth stages.
Birth is karma; this is the cause.
The body is the fruit.
Taking each moment of thought as the body:
because Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage have severed the remaining karma and remaining afflictions of the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*),
it is said that both the remainder of the birth-body (*janmakāya*) and the afflictions are completely exhausted.
Regarding those who, upon hearing the profound Dharma, do not harbor doubt or fear and are constantly able to practice it:
this clarifies that for Bodhisattvas of the Eighth Ground and above, the remaining two types of afflictions have been severed, leaving only the afflictions of momentary thought.
When the mind-made body (manomayakāya) accords with the principle of non-arising and one hears the profound and wondrous Dharma of the ninth and tenth stages,
cultivating and progressing in every thought-moment, how could there be any room for doubt or fear regarding the qualities of the mind?
The second phrase praises the internal virtues of the Mahāyāna, the magnitude of which is lofty and far-reaching;
it extends from its profound, deep, and subtle great compassion up to its being untainted by the world.
This praises the internal virtues of the Mahāyāna.
Compassion is able to uproot suffering precisely because its principle is profound and its virtue is wondrous; it is for this reason that it is so capable.
There is nothing that is not covered and sustained.
This means that once internal virtues are fully perfected, one is well able to cover and sustain all sentient beings.
To reach the other shore by means of the ultimate One Vehicle—this is the meaning.
Ultimately, through the One Vehicle within the causal stage, one reaches the further shore of Nirvana.
Regarding the phrase "the wisdom that decisively cuts through the net of doubt arises from the mind":
it refers to the wisdom that decisively cuts through the net of doubt consisting of the subtle delusions of ignorance.
The clear mirror of wisdom emerges from the mind.
Regarding the Buddhist teachings encompassing all things without exception:
the Buddha-dharma is vast and expansive, encompassing the myriad phenomena such that none are left unexhausted.
Regarding "wisdom like the great ocean," there are twenty-three similes below this that clarify the virtues of this Mahāyāna.
The profound depth and vast breadth of the ocean-like waters of internal and external transformation clarify the wondrous principles of the Mahāyāna;
these principles are so deep, moist,
and expansive that even the merit of raising a hand or bowing the head enters entirely into the ocean of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding "samādhi is like the king of mountains":
this clarifies that Mount Sumeru is composed of the seven precious jewels and is thus the sovereign of all mountains.
"Unmoved by the eight winds" clarifies that the power of concentration (*samādhi*) of this samādhi cannot be disturbed by any heterodox influences.
Regarding the phrase "from the purity of the radiance of wisdom up to the purity of universal equality":
this clarifies that the perfection and purity of the Mahāyāna radiance transcends the seven stages (*bhūmi*) of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
"Just as the great earth has no discriminatory mind toward purity or defilement,
good or evil" means that the earth can sustain all things, whether good or evil;
this illustrates how the goodness of the Mahāyāna is equal and non-dual, and how it is able to gather in and sustain sentient beings of the three vehicles.
It is like the earth, which can give birth to all things.
As for the phrase "just as pure water washes away the deep stains of worldly toil," it means that water is able to cleanse impurities.
The Mahāyāna is profound because it can remove the defilement of afflictions;
it is like a king of fire that burns away all the fuel of afflictions,
for fire is capable of incinerating wood.
This clarifies that the Dharma of the Mahāyāna can burn away the fuel of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The phrase "just as a great wind travels through all worlds without obstruction" clarifies that the Mahāyāna possesses the power of mastery, acting freely and without hindrance in every direction.
"Just as space has no attachment to anything that exists" means that this mind of equality in the Mahāyāna,
while responding to and transforming sentient beings, enters into the five desires yet remains without attachment.
It is no different from space.
As for the phrase "just as a lotus is unstained by the world," although a lotus grows in the mud, it is not defiled by that mud.
The first phrase clarifies that although Mahāyāna practitioners should teach and transform beings within the three realms and the five desires, they remain unattached to those five desires.
The third sub-phrase clarifies that Mahāyāna practitioners possess internal virtues that are fully perfected, enabling them to skillfully effect external transformation.

From its being like a Great Vehicle that carries sentient beings out of birth and death, until it reaches the point where it cannot be exhausted even after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas—
it is just like a Great Vehicle that carries sentient beings out of birth and death.
It is said to be "like" because the Mahāyāna attained by Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage has not yet reached that of a Buddha;
it clarifies that these Great Beings employ the Great Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings, transporting them across.
It causes them to be delivered from all sufferings.
Just as thick clouds thunder the great Dharma-thunder to awaken those who are not yet awakened,
for clouds are able to provide shelter and shade for all things.
Just as thunder can produce a resonant sound that startles and moves the hearts of sentient beings,
so too does the Bodhisattva internally take compassion as their protective canopy and externally employ the four analytical knowledges to attract and guide others.
It is like the thundering sound of a peal of thunder;
it is like a great rain showering down the nectar of the Dharma to moisten sentient beings,
just as the rain from heaven nourishes sprouts and shoots.
This is because the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma moistens and benefits sentient beings.
As for the analogy of the Vajra Mountain, which all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cannot move despite their rubbing against it,
this clarifies that the vajra is capable of shattering all things.
The vajra-like wisdom of the bodhisattva can shatter the myriad delusions.
As for the statement that it is like the nyagrodha tree which universally covers all,
this clarifies that the Mahāyāna is equal and universally covers all sentient beings.
"Like the garuḍa bird, which subdues non-Buddhists through its majesty" means that it is like a bodhisattva subduing non-Buddhists through his majesty.
"Like various wandering birds, which leave no trace of their path" means—
The principle of the Mahāyāna is equal and impartial.
It is like wild birds and beasts that have no place of concealment;
if there were a place of concealment, it would be partiality.
Regarding the phrase "like a bull king because none can surpass him":
the "country" refers to the Bodhisattva, who, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, excels those below.
The "elephant king" clarifies that the power of the Bodhisattva is great.
"Like the lion king" clarifies fearless preaching.
"Vast as empty space" refers to...
This clarifies that the mind of Mahāyāna carries beings across with a vastness equal to space.
To cultivate the six points of harmonious respect means to purify one’s body,
speech, mind, intentions, views, and offerings of food and clothing to others.
These six points share a single intent:
the dharma for those who have left the household life is that each and every person should consult and receive instruction from one another with minds free of obstruction.
If there is even the slightest obstacle of pride or wealth, the sixfold harmony (*ṣaḍ-vidha-sāmīcī*) will not be accomplished.
"Extinguishing the three defilements and hindrances" means extinguishing the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
"The power of the cause" refers to...
The eighth stage clarifies that Bodhisattvas constantly transform and receive sentient beings through the Mahāyāna.
Initially, they awaken the dispositions of beings, who establish names according to their respective objects;
therefore, this is called "the power of causes."

The Great Being (Mahāsattva) is essentially a single body of wisdom; its depth or shallowness varies according to the objects it encounters, and its designations are likewise assigned in accordance with those objects.
As for "the power of conditions":
It acts as an external condition to cause the spiritual understanding of sentient beings to increase for a time, providing them with swift nourishment.
As for "the power of intention" (*manas-bala*), it clarifies that the mental ground constantly seeks the virtuous opportunities of sentient beings, desiring to receive them.
As for the power of the vow (*praṇidhāna-bala*): it clarifies that the Bodhisattva possesses a profound vow to deliver all sentient beings.
As for the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*):
Skillful means refers to the cleverness of speech used to deliver sentient beings.
Constant power refers to the constant desire to deliver sentient beings.
Regarding the power of goodness (*śubhabala*):
all the powers mentioned above are entirely wholesome. Regarding the power of meditative concentration (*samādhibala*):
To remain undisturbed amidst sensory objects.
As for the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*):
wisdom has the meaning of contemplative observation.
It illuminates the myriad realms.
As for the power of extensive learning,
the capacities and conditions of sentient beings are not uniform.
Because one desires to hear various teachings of the Dharma, the name is established based on the object;
thus, it is the power of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).
This applies to those who practice generosity, ethical discipline, and patience.
The six pāramitās are used to transform sentient beings.
This right mindfulness encourages the practice of the ten recollections so that they may be born in that land.
Śamatha and vipaśyanā are the primary gateway for those first entering meditative concentration.
As for the powers of the various supernormal knowledges and clarities:
"Abhijñā" refers to the six superknowledges;
"vidyā" refers to the three insights.
As for the power of one who, having disciplined themselves according to the Dharma, subdues all sentient beings: it is as follows.
It is for the sake of transforming those who are stubborn and violent. Thus,
one subdues them with firmness and only then causes them to receive the True Dharma.
Those who are gentle and compliant are transformed by soft speech.
Thus, he is fully endowed with all such powers.
This summary of the various powers clarifies that the Bodhisattva possesses them all.
Those who are constantly praised by all Buddhas are those bodhisattvas who have planted causes for a long time and made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas;
it is for this reason that they have attained such powers.
Regarding the various gates of samādhi that are neither arising nor ceasing:
since they are the principle of emptiness and non-arising,
how could they admit of a mind subject to arising and ceasing?
To realize this principle such that it is tranquil and undisturbed is samādhi;
samādhi is concentration.
Having accomplished immeasurable merit, it cannot be exhausted.
Having concluded the praise of the internal virtues of the Mahāyāna and the various powers of its external transformation,
this is the summary of those powers.
The fifth section extensively clarifies gain and loss and exhorts practice.
It begins with the Buddha’s address to Maitreya Bodhisattva, the devas, humans, and others, concluding with the words: "I shall practice according to the teaching and dare not harbor any doubt."
To clarify the distinction between gain and loss, [the Buddha] further cites the bodhisattvas, devas, and humans of that land, as well as its wondrous realm, to Maitreya.
These beings ought to attain such [realization], yet they remain greedily attached to the five desires.
They quarrel over wealth and property;
thus, they show no sense of righteousness toward their parents and brothers,
failing to realize that they should renounce such attachments to cultivate goodness.
These are the six errors.
Within this chapter, there are further four sub-sections.
The first sub-section extends from the beginning up to the point where men and women together grieve over wealth.
Regarding those whose merit and wisdom are beyond description:
wishing first to lament what they have lost,
one first lauds the fruit of that which was lost.
What is the fruit?
It is the Bodhisattva and the Pure Land.
Why do you not strive to do good and contemplate the spontaneity of the Way?
This encourages one to cultivate the causes to attain the fruit of Buddhahood through spontaneity (*svayambhū*).
Regarding the phrase "clinging to neither the upper nor the lower,
penetrating without limit," the scriptural text should actually read "not clinging to the upper or the lower."
The luminous essence of spontaneity, though it manifests within the six realms of existence among humans and devas, remains unstained and unattached.
Its profound discernment of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—is inexhaustible;
therefore, it is said to penetrate all things without limit.
However, as for the understanding that [the inhabitants] dwell above and below,
this clarifies that in that land,
the fruit of retribution is such that there is no separation between gods and humans by way of the Form or Desire Realms.
The heavens also descend below,
and humans likewise ascend to the heavens;
the lands are interconnected and free from obstruction.
Because they exercise sovereign mastery over the upper and lower realms with total freedom, it is said that they penetrate to the boundless limits.
Each of you should diligently apply yourselves with vigor and exertion to seek this for yourselves; those who dwell in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing shall attain rebirth there.
Exhorting them to diligently apply themselves to cultivate the causes so that they will surely attain the wondrous fruit;
"crossing transversely through the five evil paths so that they naturally close" means that through diligent application and exertion,
one cultivates goodness until it becomes increasingly bright and clear.
One will no longer undergo rebirth within the five realms of existence; likewise, the evil paths are all closed off.
As for "ascending the Way without end":
because the wondrous principle leads to a sublime ascent into a land that is truly pure and as vast as the boundless, it is said to be without end.
That which is easy to traverse yet no one does is the practice of the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*, which is difficult to encourage others to practice;
whereas by the power of ten recitations, it is easy to encourage others to practice.
Even within that which is easy,
if one practices the ten recitations, one may not achieve even a single successful recitation.
If, however, one achieves success in practicing the ten recitations, or even just a single recitation, [then...]
One will then attain rebirth in the Pure Land;
because they are unable to achieve [the necessary conditions],
it is said that "it is easy to go, yet there are no people."
That land does not oppose or contravene what is led by the natural order.
This clarifies that in that pure land, there are no sufferings of the five realms of existence to conflict with a virtuous mind;
rather, it is solely because of the natural, wondrous goodness and the constant provision of excellence that one is led by these words.
Why not abandon worldly affairs so as to attain unsurpassed bliss?
I urge you to cultivate goodness so that you may be reborn in a pure land with a lifespan extending through distant kalpas.
Yet, people of this world are shallow and vulgar, contending over matters that are not urgent.
It is clear that people of shallow character have little instruction in the Way and do not recognize conditioned existence or impermanence;
they only contend over matters of no urgency, thereby further increasing their heavy transgressions.
Thus, the Sages exhorted them, saying:
Why not cultivate the ten recollections without contention?
By recollecting Amitāyus Buddha of the West,
one will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Those who have neither honor nor humility dwell amidst heavy delusions, taking suffering for pleasure;
they do not recognize that suffering is something to be loathed.
Furthermore, by what means can one recognize that enlightenment is worthy of veneration?
The second phrase clarifies that there is no need for exhortation to practice it.
From the point where existence and non-existence are alike and sorrowful reflection is equal, there is no one who can know it.
The reason for clarifying existence and non-existence is to clarify that sentient beings are entangled by delusions and do not recognize that conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
One simply knows that there is a field and thus worries about the field; there is a house and thus worries about the house; everything below is like this.
From the beginning until "it pains those who dwell therein," it clarifies that one already possesses a field and therefore worries about it.
The passage beginning with "From poverty, inferiority, and constant destitution" clarifies that one lacks fields and houses and is further distressed by the desire to possess them.
The third phrase clarifies the lack of meaningful purpose and exhorts [the practitioner] to cultivate [virtue].
From the people of the world—fathers, sons, and brothers—what joy do they seek?
They should instead cultivate mutual respect and affection, refraining from hatred and envy;
they should be encouraged to practice virtue, study propriety and righteousness, and recognize the distinctions between the honorable and the humble, the superior and the inferior.
Together they shall cultivate the path of goodness and be reborn in the land of the Western Pure Land.
As for those who harbor anger and resentment in this life, harboring even slight feelings of hatred and jealousy that will become more severe in future lives—
This clarifies that those who lack righteous purpose incur immeasurable and grave offenses in the present life through mutual hatred and jealousy;
in future lives, they will become increasingly deluded and enter the three miserable realms and the hells.
There is no rest. The fourth phrase clarifies the exhortation to practice for those who lack faith:
from "In this way, people do not believe that performing good deeds brings good results" up to "the pain is unspeakable; they are truly to be pitied."
"Not believing that after death one is reborn" refers to a lack of faith regarding the fruit [of actions].
"That through generous giving one obtains merit" [refers to faith in the cause].
This refers to a lack of faith during the causal stage.
To have no faith whatsoever in matters of good and evil means to lack faith in both good and evil.
As for those who say "it is not so," it is because in reality one obtains good by practicing virtue and gains merit through giving; yet,
because they do not believe that practicing virtue brings merit, they say, "it is not so."
Otherwise, it is merely another name for "lack of faith"; in the end,
there is nothing of the sort that exists.
This clarifies that those who do not believe will ultimately never cultivate goodness or obtain blessings.

As for the phrase "merely because of this, one sees it for oneself," it means that because one's former teachers and ancestors practiced non-belief, they were consequently led to see and practice [the results of] such conduct.
Seeing that this practice follows the conduct of former masters, they do not believe it;
looking at one another, those before and after are likewise the same.
This species of non-believers, having inherited and transmitted it from previous lives to subsequent ones, continue to practice evil without change.
Therefore, it is said that they are all alike.
Being unable to see for themselves, they have no words [of reproach];
they do not recognize their own grave evils.
