Furthermore, there are no virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra) to speak to them and urge them to cultivate goodness.
Regarding good fortune and misfortune, calamity and blessing, they each act according to their own impulses; not one among them finds anything strange about this.
There are no virtuous friends to tell them of these fortunes and misfortunes so that they might diligently study and practice accordingly.
Sixth, the clarification of the exhortation to practice through discernment:

From the Buddha’s address to Maitreya Bodhisattva, “O devas, humans, and others, I have now finished speaking to you,” down to “I shall respectfully receive and practice these four teachings, not daring to harbor any doubt.”
That which clarifies "discernment" (viveka) means to eliminate all that is evil and to select and take up all that is sublime and good.
Those who select what is good and practice it with diligence are encouraged to abandon evil and cultivate virtue; the world honors them.
All things are impermanent;
it is not like cultivating even a single hair’s breadth of goodness, which will surely lead one away from the suffering of birth and death.
Do not follow your own whims and allow yourself to fall behind others by violating the sutras and precepts.
Exhort and urge them to study so that they may distance themselves from the five desires,
causing their roots of goodness to increase day and night;
do not allow them to fall behind others.
Those who encounter the Buddha and listen to and receive the Dharma have planted the causes for this over a long period of time.
Now that they have met the Buddha, he exhorts them to listen to the Dharma, stirring their hearts at this critical moment.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "How joyful and excellent it is to hear of Amitāyus Buddha":
at that time, the assembly heard that the long life and wondrous bliss of that Buddha’s land were so perfectly suited to their hearts' desire that they exclaimed, "How joyful and excellent!"
To long cultivate the Way and its virtue so as to become enlightened means that,
once born in the Pure Land, one dwells in goodness with a refined and liberated spirit;
to harmonize with the principle of non-arising is what constitutes true illumination.
Regarding those who are next to the path of *nirvāṇa*:
because Maitreya and others, being bodhisattvas in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), are adjacent to the realm of the Buddha, they are said to be "next to the path of *nirvāṇa*."
Do not harbor doubts or feel regret.
Between the eyebrows of Amitāyus Buddha is a white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*), curling gracefully like five Mount Sumerus.
When sentient beings see this white tuft, they may give rise to doubt and say:
If one harbors such doubts as to whether this white tuft of hair belongs to Amitāyus Buddha or is merely a fabrication,
after death they will be reborn in the Western Land within the City of Doubt; there,
their lotus flower will close over their head and never open.
One practices the path of repentance within this lotus flower;
only after five hundred years have passed does the lotus flower finally open,
allowing one to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
Although they see the Buddha and hear the Dharma, they do so without clear understanding;
yet, despite this lack of clarity, they gradually awaken to the Path.
Those born in that borderland in halls made of the seven treasures—
This arises from doubt; although the people within the city have this doubt, because their vow to be born in that land is strong,
they succeed in being born there through the power of that vow.
Because of their doubt, they are unable to approach the Buddha;
they can only enter the periphery of that Buddha’s realm and dwell within a lotus flower.
Since the lotus flower closes at its head and does not open, it is said that they are born in the borderlands.
Seventh, the clarification of the refutation of the five precepts and the exhortation to practice.
From the Buddha’s address to Maitreya, "Thus, etc., one is able in this world," it specifically intends to clarify the five pains and the five burnings.
First, the characteristics of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions are explained in detail.
These five precepts and ten wholesome actions are all fully endowed with the three wholesome roots of the mental faculty: non-greed, non-delusion, and non-hatred.
Cultivating the ten wholesome actions subverts the ten unwholesome actions, and cultivating the five precepts subverts the five unwholesome actions.
These five precepts constitute the lay discipline (*gṛhastha-saṃvara*).
Generally speaking, "discipline" refers to the weighing of light and heavy [offenses].
Now, regarding what is called the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*):
"precept" (*śīla*) takes the non-arising of mental evil as its meaning.
The meaning of the non-arising of mental evil is that within the sphere of one's own mind, evil does not arise; this is itself the goodness of the mind.
Furthermore, being able to transform others externally is precisely the practice of goodness.
This precept is also called "that," and that liberation is also called "the matter."
Is one liberated from [the abstention from] killing? No.
One is not liberated from the side of abstaining from killing, up to and including the side of abstaining from drinking alcohol;
rather, one is liberated from the side of abstaining from drinking alcohol.
However, sentient beings, with their heavy burden of deceit and delusion, violate and break the five precepts,
giving rise to the five evils and even the five burnings.
Within this chapter, there are seven sections that clarify these meanings.
The first section provides a general explanation of the violation of the five precepts;
this refers to the "five pains and five burnings.
It begins with "One who is thus able, in this world, to maintain an upright mind and correct intention," and concludes with "the path to long life and nirvana."

Those who are able to maintain an upright mind and correct intention in this world, such as these, will be free from the greed, hatred, and delusion of the mental ground; being thus free from these, they shall be without manifold evils.
Because they are without manifold evils, inner virtues will arise.
He who is most peerless throughout the worlds of the ten directions is one who is free from greed, hatred,
and delusion; because such a being does not exist in the world, he is without equal.
Why is this so? To explain the reason why the mental ground is free from greed, hatred, and delusion:
it is simply because one cultivates what is wholesome and abandons what is unwholesome that there is no greed, hatred, or delusion.
As for those who naturally perform wholesome deeds:
in that land, the devas and humans are free from the three poisons and possess only pure goodness.
"Those who can easily attain awakening are those who have entered into principle; they are easily transformed by the Way.
Now, I have become a Buddha in this world to dwell among those who suffer from the five evils."
Śākyamuni himself clarified that the land he attained was one where sentient beings were defiled and evil, taking the three poisons and four inversions as their afflictions; for this reason,
he established the five precepts to counteract the five evils.
These five evils are the causes for the arising of evil.
What are the five?
First is killing living beings.
Second is stealing;
third is covetousness;
fourth is false speech.
Fifth is drinking alcohol.
These five evils are the causes from past times that can extinguish the present;
they are the fruits of the five pains and five burnings.
The five types of suffering are the results in the present life;
because the cause was evil, the result is suffering.
Because the afflictions burn intensely and scorch their own characteristics, they are called the "five pains.
The "five burnings" refer to the fruits of the future.
Since the present fruit is not real,
the future must consequently be subject to annihilation and total extinction.
To teach and transform sentient beings so that they may abandon the five evils—
Exhorting others to cultivate goodness causes them to abandon the five evils.
Since the causes of evil no longer arise,
they will likewise not experience the fruits of the five pains and five burnings.
"To subdue and transform their minds so that they may uphold the five virtues" means to cause them to uphold the goodness of the five precepts.
"The way of transcending the world, long life, and nirvana" refers to the path [leading to these].
This is the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The second section clarifies how killing violates the precept against killing;
it begins from "One evil act" and concludes with "this constitutes one great good."
Within this section, five subordinate phrases clarify the meaning.
The first subordinate phrase clarifies the past causes for committing killing,
from the words "from one who is evil" up to "the transgressor."
"Not killing even crawling insects" and "desiring to commit various evils, there is none that is not thus"—
these clarify the commission of evil deeds in the past.
Because sentient beings practice the evil karma of killing,
they receive in the present life the retribution of a short lifespan and incomplete six sense faculties.
This applies to those who injure, harm, or slaughter others.
Not knowing how to reverse the flow and exhaust the source,
they harbor only thoughts of slaughter;
this is the cause for creating the hells.
Regarding those who, having committed evil and rebellious acts contrary to the Way, subsequently receive calamity and punishment:
this refers to the fact that because they created causes for evil in the past, they will inevitably receive the retribution of poverty, low status, and inferiority in the present.
The second phrase clarifies the reception of other karmic fruits in the present life.
From those who are poor and lowly down to those who do not even attain [basic sustenance],
these eight subsequent phrases clarify the certainty of the remaining results in the present life.
This is because in a previous existence they committed the evil karma of killing and failed to practice giving.
They merely plundered the property of others;
for this reason, they fell into hell.
Once their punishment was completed, the remaining karmic retribution was not yet exhausted.
Now one has received a human body;
yet, despite having obtained a human body, one may be deaf, blind, mute, or dumb, with the six sense faculties incomplete.
The third phrase clarifies that by practicing wholesome deeds, one obtains the noble fruit of rebirth.
From those who are noble and honorable down to those who receive their bodies through successive transmigration,
there are also those who are noble, wealthy, of high talent, and profoundly enlightened.
This is because they have practiced wholesome causes with clear understanding and thus obtained wholesome fruits.
"That all is due to the cultivation of virtuous merit through compassion and filial piety in past lives" clarifies that by practicing these causes of compassion and filial piety in the past,
one now obtains the retributive fruits of nobility and great wealth in the present.
The fourth phrase provides a simile for those who are deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired, illustrating how they receive retribution across two lifetimes.
From the passage beginning with "For example, like the suffering of the king’s law" up until "one pain and one burning; such is the diligent suffering."
First, it is like the law of a king where the most extreme punishment is meted out to a criminal;
this clarifies that those who are deaf, blind, mute, or speech-impaired manifest the retribution of extremely heavy suffering in the present life.
Thus, there are those who naturally undergo immeasurable afflictions within the three miserable realms.
Having already experienced suffering in the present, one will further undergo the heavy sufferings of the three miserable realms in future lives.
Regarding "exchanging and trading their bodies":
because they receive the bodies of the six destinies not just once but repeatedly, it is said that they "exchange and trade their bodies."

Those who have altered their punishments and changed their ways have already completed [their retribution] and received bodies within the six realms; the evil paths they practice are likewise the same.
As for the length of the lifespans they receive, whether long or short—
The forms received within the six realms of existence differ, and the karma created through one's conduct likewise differs;
therefore, lifespans vary in length.
The fifth phrase clarifies the conclusion of the exhortation.
From the simile of a great fire that has finished burning a person's body, this constitutes one great "clear light" (*suvimalāloka*).
This is an exhortation to practice:
if one can diligently cultivate and exert oneself, [one will attain it].
One will then attain the unconditioned path of Nirvana.
If one is unable to practice and gives rise to evil,
one will fall into the three miserable realms, like a person being consumed by a great fire.
The third section clarifies the violation of the precept against stealing through the act of theft.
It begins from the Buddha’s words, “These two are evils,” and concludes with, “These are the two great virtues.
Within this section, there are five subordinate phrases that clarify the meaning.
The first section clarifies the causes of theft.

From the Buddha’s statement, "These two evils... up to "...there is nothing to rely upon," the meaning of these phrases within this section on theft is no different from that of the preceding chapter.
The second and third phrases clarify both [aspects] together.
From "coming alone and going alone with not a single follower" until "when the matter arrives, one regrets; good and evil, calamity and blessing, follow the life to its place of rebirth."
This clarifies both the good causes and good effects, as well as the evil causes and evil effects.
As for "being in a place of happiness," this refers to the good effects.
"Or entering into bitter poison" refers to the fruit of suffering.
This fourth phrase serves as a simile for the person who previously committed evil deeds.
From the present life, including the existing royal laws and prisons, up to the two pains, the two burnings, and such diligent suffering—
this clarifies the suffering of the two worlds. In the present,
one undergoes the suffering of the five dharmas.
In future lives, one will undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms.
The fifth phrase clarifies the concluding exhortation,
beginning from "For example, as a great fire burns the human body" and ending with "the two great evils."
The fourth section clarifies how lustful desire violates the precept against sexual misconduct.
It begins from the Buddha’s words, "As for those three evils," and concludes with "these are the three great virtues.
Within this section, there are four sub-phrases that clarify the meaning.
The first phrase clarifies the cause of lustful desire;
from the beginning until "merely wishing to obtain it in vain," it explains this.
The second phrase clarifies the cause and effect of committing evil deeds.
From "glancing at those with subtle physical ailments" onwards, it describes how one afflicts such people.

The third phrase clarifies that one subsequently undergoes the bitter retribution of the three miserable realms (*durgati*). From "furthermore, not fearing the prohibitions of the five dharmas" until "the three pains and three burnings; such is the diligent suffering," [it continues].
Regarding those humans or spirits who are possessed by such evil:
having committed such grave offenses,
their names may be inscribed [in the registers].
Alternatively, one may be among humans with incomplete six sense-faculties,
or one may be among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The fourth section clarifies the exhortation and conclusion.
From the analogy of a great fire burning a person’s body until the end of the four great virtues;
the fifth section clarifies how false speech destroys the precept of truthful speech.
From the Buddha’s statement regarding the four evils until the conclusion, "these are the four great virtues."
Within this section, there are five sub-sections.
The first sub-section clarifies the causes of false speech,
from the words of the Buddha regarding the four evils up to the statement that it is difficult to attain sincerity and truthfulness.
The second phrase clarifies the evil results,
from noble arrogance up to the divine records and consciousness.
The third phrase clarifies the cultivation of wholesome causes.
The third phrase clarifies that those who have previously performed some meritorious deeds will receive protection and assistance.
The fourth phrase clarifies that sentient beings who commit evil will receive the retribution of the three miserable realms and the hells in future lives.
From "In this life, having committed evil, one's merit perishes of its own accord" until "the four pains and four burnings,
such is the diligent suffering," the fifth phrase clarifies the exhortation and conclusion.
From "For example, like a great fire burning a person's body" until "the four great elements are good," [the text concludes].
The sixth section clarifies how drinking alcohol violates the precept against drinking.
From the Buddha’s statement regarding the five evils up to "this constitutes the five great virtues," this section elucidates its meaning through six sub-sentences.
The first phrase clarifies the preliminary means for drinking alcohol.
From the Buddha’s statement regarding the five evils down to the point of using it for one's own sustenance,
one specifically intends to drink alcohol and first employs the preparatory means for drinking alcohol.
This constitutes the actual transgression of the precept-body.
The second phrase clarifies that drinking alcohol is a cause of evil.
This extends from indulging in wine and craving fine flavors up to [neglecting] one's parents, siblings, and kinsmen.
The third phrase clarifies the retribution for committing evil:
from being loathed by one's six kin, one will never attain liberation or release.
Such is the state of those whose minds and intentions are likewise [corrupt].
The sixth relative and all worldly people share the same intention and wish for his death; therefore, it is said that "mind and intent are both thus.
The fourth phrase clarifies the cause and effect of wholesome karma.
"Those who are good people and practice goodness clarify and cultivate wholesome causes.
From happiness they enter happiness; from clarity they enter clarity."
This is the good fruit.
The fifth phrase clarifies that those who commit evil will receive the retribution of heavy suffering and craving in future lives.
